FuTransformer: FP8 Prefill and INT4 Decode for Llama-Style Inference on Hopper

 

Wei Wang 

wei.wang217@gmail.com

††footnotetext: Correspondence to: Wei Wang <wei.wang217@gmail.com>.
Abstract

Transformer inference has different bottlenecks during prefill and decode. Prefill reuses weights across many tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement. Single-token decode has limited data reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FuTransformer, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. CODA showed how to express Transformer training operators as GEMM-plus-epilogue programs. FuTransformer applies this principle to inference. It adds direct KV-cache placement, folds the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writes FP8 values directly from the producing epilogue using delayed scaling, and supports prefill without padding. For decode, FuTransformer uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 copy of the KV cache. Keys and weights follow the Tensor Core fragment layout, so the kernels can dequantize them directly into MMA operands without creating full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform makes INT4 cache quantization less sensitive to outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48×\times faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For the closest shared operation, gate/up projection followed by SwiGLU, the BF16 path is 1.13×\times faster than the released CODA kernel at the 8B shape. Our FP8 inference path is 2.02–2.18×\times faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across the 8B and 70B shapes at batch 1 to 32, INT4 decode is 1.3–2.4×\times faster than whichever PyTorch decode block is faster at each point: 2.1–3.3×\times faster than the compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 block, and 1.3–6.3×\times faster than the same block using PyTorch’s INT4 projection kernel, which is built for a single query row and loses to its own BF16 block at batch 32. INT4 decode is also 31–51% faster than our FP8 decode path. For the complete Llama-3.1-8B model, one INT4 decode step takes 2.8 ms at batch one, compared with 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. On Llama-3.1-8B, decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path increases perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights, or to 6.99 with GPTQ weights stored in the same format. The rotated INT4 cache adds another 0.20. The kernel path matches the quantized reference computation to within 0.001 perplexity.

1 Introduction

Matrix multiplication dominates Transformer FLOPs, but data movement and other operations also contribute to execution time. A decoder block also performs normalization, residual updates, position encoding, activation functions, precision conversion, and KV-cache updates. These operations perform little arithmetic but often read and write large intermediate tensors. As Tensor Cores become faster, this data movement takes a larger share of the total execution time.

CODA Guo et al. (2026) addresses this problem for training by expressing many Transformer operators as GEMM-plus-epilogue programs. An optimized GEMM mainloop produces an output tile. A programmable epilogue then processes the tile while it is still on chip. This allows pairwise operations such as RoPE and SwiGLU, as well as residual updates, scaling, and partial reductions, to run without separate reads and writes to global memory.

FuTransformer uses the same GEMM-plus-epilogue principle for autoregressive inference. Inference adds two requirements. First, prefill must manage persistent state. It must write K and V directly to the KV cache, produce low-precision activations for later projections, and support requests of different lengths. Second, decode has too few rows to behave like a large GEMM. At small batch sizes, each layer reads its weights for only a few rows, and attention reads cached K and V values for every query. The decode path must therefore reduce the bytes read and prevent dequantization from delaying the main computation.

For prefill, FuTransformer uses persistent FP8 GEMMs with epilogue policies selected at compile time. These policies apply RoPE or SwiGLU, write K and V to the cache, collect RMSNorm statistics, restore scales, and optionally write FP8 output directly. Inference weights are fixed, so the learned RMSNorm gain can be folded into the next projection before quantization. The row-wise normalization factor is then applied in that projection’s epilogue. This removes the normalized activation tensor while preserving the quantized computation. Packed inputs also remove padded projection rows from batches with different request lengths.

For decode, FuTransformer uses INT4 weights and an INT4 copy of the KV cache. Hopper has no INT4 Tensor Core MMA, and its FP8 MMA requires large warpgroup shapes that the few query rows in decode cannot fill. The kernel must therefore expand INT4 values before a 16-bit MMA. The main design choice is where to perform this expansion. FuTransformer stores keys and weights in the order required by the MMA fragments. A byte-indexed lookup converts packed cache values into FP16 pairs. A short sequence of logic and packed BF16 operations converts weight nibbles directly in registers. Group scales are applied after accumulation. Before cache quantization, a block-diagonal Hadamard transform spreads large channel values. Matching transforms on the query and attention output preserve the attention computation before quantization.

The main contributions are:

  • •

    Inference-specific GEMM epilogues. Starting from CODA’s GEMM-plus-epilogue formulation, FuTransformer adds direct KV-cache placement, folds the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writes FP8 producer output with delayed scaling, and supports packed prefill.

  • •

    Fragment-aligned INT4 decode. INT4 weights and cache entries are packed in the layout required by the MMA fragments that consume them. Values are dequantized in registers or through a small lookup table. Scales are applied outside the per-element inner loop.

  • •

    Outlier-aware cache quantization. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces INT4 cache error when keys contain large channel outliers. Before quantization, the transform preserves the exact attention dot product.

  • •

    A final-result evaluation. We compare full prefill and decode layers with PyTorch. We also compare the complete Llama-3.1-8B model with PyTorch and the closest shared gate/up–SwiGLU stage with CODA. We report performance and numerical error, and label comparisons that use different precisions. Using a trained Llama-3.1-8B checkpoint, we decode every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 path and measure perplexity, per-layer error, and error accumulated across layers.

2 Background and Positioning

2.1 Llama-style inference block

Let X∈ℝM×HX\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times H} contain MM token vectors, each with hidden width HH. Let II denote the feed-forward width, HqH_{q} the number of query heads, Hk​vH_{kv} the number of KV heads, and DD the head dimension. We evaluate this block:

X^\displaystyle\widehat{X} =RMSNorm⁡(X,γ1),\displaystyle=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X;\gamma_{1}),
(Q,K,V)\displaystyle(Q,K,V) =X^​Wq​k​v⊤,\displaystyle=\widehat{X}W_{qkv}^{\top}, (1)
O\displaystyle O =Attention⁡(RoPE⁡(Q),Kc,Vc),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Attention}(\operatorname{RoPE}(Q),K_{c},V_{c}),
X1\displaystyle X_{1} =X+O​Wo⊤,\displaystyle=X+OW_{o}^{\top}, (2)
X^1\displaystyle\widehat{X}_{1} =RMSNorm⁡(X1;γ2),\displaystyle=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X_{1};\gamma_{2}),
Z\displaystyle Z =SiLU⁡(X^1​Wg⊤)⊙(X^1​Wu⊤),\displaystyle=\operatorname{SiLU}(\widehat{X}_{1}W_{g}^{\top})\odot(\widehat{X}_{1}W_{u}^{\top}), (3)
Y\displaystyle Y =X1+Z​Wd⊤.\displaystyle=X_{1}+ZW_{d}^{\top}. (4)

KcK_{c} and VcV_{c} store the keys and values for earlier tokens and the current token. The block uses causal grouped-query attention (GQA) Ainslie et al. (2023) and RMSNorm Zhang and Sennrich (2019). The gate and up projections share one GEMM, giving four projection GEMMs and one attention stage in total.

During prefill, M=B​SM=BS, where BB is the batch size and SS is the sequence length. Each weight tile is reused across many token rows. During single-token decode, M=BM=B. At the small batch sizes studied here, reading the weights accounts for most projection latency. Attention latency grows with context length TT because attention must read the KV cache.

2.2 GEMM-plus-epilogue programs and CODA

A high-performance GEMM has two parts. The mainloop loads input tiles and performs matrix multiply-accumulate operations. The epilogue processes and stores each completed output tile. At that point, the output is already in registers or shared memory. The epilogue can therefore perform local operations without first writing an intermediate tensor to HBM.

CODA Guo et al. (2026) provides a structured way to use this idea in Transformer training. It keeps the GEMM mainloop fixed and offers five groups of epilogue operations that can be combined: elementwise and pairwise maps; vector loads and stores; tile loads and stores; tile reductions, with partial results combined by a small auxiliary kernel; and stateful transforms. CODA also shows that the row-wise RMSNorm factor can be moved through the following GEMM and applied in its epilogue. Together, these operations cover nearly all non-attention work in the forward and backward passes of a Transformer block.

FlashAttention introduced tiled attention designed to reduce data movement, together with online softmax. Later work adapted the execution schedule to newer GPU pipelines and low precision Dao et al. (2022); Dao (2024); Shah et al. (2024). FuTransformer’s prefill attention follows this approach. Its decode design focuses on how low-bit K and V values are stored and expanded into the MMA fragments that use them.

2.3 Low-precision weights and KV caches

FP8 E4M3 reduces the data read and written by projections while retaining Tensor Core execution Micikevicius and others (2022). If Am​k≈am​Am​kqA_{mk}\approx a_{m}A^{q}_{mk} and Wn​k≈bn​Wn​kqW_{nk}\approx b_{n}W^{q}_{nk}, then

C~m​n=am​bn​∑kAm​kq​Wn​kq.\widetilde{C}_{mn}=a_{m}b_{n}\sum_{k}A^{q}_{mk}W^{q}_{nk}. (5)

The row and column scales can be applied after accumulation, rather than to every product. Systems such as Transformer Engine use delayed scaling NVIDIA (2026b): the producer writes FP8 output immediately, using a scale collected during an earlier execution.

GPTQ and AWQ made group-scaled INT4 weights practical Frantar et al. (2023); Lin and others (2024). Marlin showed the benefits of packing weights in Tensor Core fragment order and dequantizing them in registers Frantar et al. (2024). KIVI studied low-bit KV caches Liu et al. (2024). QuaRot and SAW-INT4 use Hadamard rotations to reduce activation and cache outliers Ashkboos and others (2024); Jia et al. (2026). FuTransformer combines these ideas in a complete Hopper decode block, with layouts designed for its attention and projection fragments.

3 FuTransformer Design

3.1 Overview

FuTransformer uses separate prefill and decode paths because they have different bottlenecks. Prefill keeps large GEMMs efficient and reduces data movement between them. Decode reduces the bytes read for weights and the cache, then dequantizes values in the layout required by the MMA operands.

The prefill projection kernel uses 128×256×128128\times 256\times 128 CTA tiles, a four-stage TMA pipeline, one producer warpgroup, and two consumer warpgroups. Its mainloop uses Hopper FP8 WGMMA and the Tensor Memory Accelerator NVIDIA (2026a). An epilogue policy selected at compile time controls how each completed fragment is processed and stored. The QKV, output, gate/up, and down projections can therefore perform different inference operations while sharing one optimized GEMM mainloop.

The decode path has two kernel families. A register-streaming kernel handles M=1M=1, and a skinny matrix kernel handles 2≤M≤322\leq M\leq 32. Both read packed INT4 weights and expand them directly into MMA fragments for accumulation with BF16 activations. Decode attention reads the INT4 cache copy. For long contexts, it uses split-KV reduction.

3.2 Inference-aware FP8 prefill

3.2.1 Direct KV-cache placement

In training, K and V are activations used later in the same pass. In inference, they must be written to persistent cache addresses. A conventional implementation first writes dense K and V tensors, then launches another kernel to scatter them into the cache. FuTransformer writes them to the cache directly from the QKV epilogue.

For each output row mm, metadata gives the request and token position pmp_{m}. The epilogue maps each output column to a head and channel in Q, K, or V. It restores the projection scales, applies RoPE to Q and K, writes Q in the layout used by attention, and stores K and V at

offset⁡(request⁡(m),head,pm,channel).\operatorname{offset}(\operatorname{request}(m),\operatorname{head},p_{m},\operatorname{channel}). (6)

Each cache element has one writer, and elements outside the valid range are masked. This removes the dense K/V intermediate tensors and the separate cache-scatter pass.

3.2.2 Folding the frozen RMSNorm gain

The block applies RMSNorm before the QKV and gate/up projections. Define

qm=∑hxm​h2,ρm=(qm/H+ϵ)−1/2.q_{m}=\sum_{h}x_{mh}^{2},\qquad\rho_{m}=\left(q_{m}/H+\epsilon\right)^{-1/2}. (7)

For projection weight row WnW_{n} and learned gain γ\gamma, the output is

Cm​n\displaystyle C_{mn} =∑hxm​h​ρm​γh​Wn​h=ρm​∑hxm​h​Wn​h′,\displaystyle=\sum_{h}x_{mh}\rho_{m}\gamma_{h}W_{nh}=\rho_{m}\sum_{h}x_{mh}W^{\prime}_{nh},
Wn​h′\displaystyle W^{\prime}_{nh} =γh​Wn​h.\displaystyle=\gamma_{h}W_{nh}. (8)

CODA moves the row factor ρm\rho_{m} through the next GEMM and applies it in that GEMM’s epilogue. During inference, γ\gamma and WW are fixed. FuTransformer therefore folds γ\gamma into WW once, before quantizing and repacking the weights. The GEMM then reads the raw activation XX and the preprocessed weight W′W^{\prime}. With FP8 operands, the output is

C~m​n=ρm​am​bn​∑hXm​hq​(W′)n​hq.\widetilde{C}_{mn}=\rho_{m}a_{m}b_{n}\sum_{h}X^{q}_{mh}(W^{\prime})^{q}_{nh}. (9)

The epilogue that produces the residual stream also computes partial sums of squares. A small reduction combines the results from all output tiles to obtain qmq_{m}. The next projection uses ρm\rho_{m}, so no normalized activation tensor needs to be written to HBM.

3.2.3 Delayed FP8 emission

The down projection reads the SwiGLU output ZZ. If the gate/up epilogue writes this output in BF16, a separate quantization kernel must read it and write an FP8 copy. For MM rows and feed-forward width II, the two approaches move

ℬseparate=5​M​I,ℬproducer=M​I,\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{separate}}=5MI,\qquad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{producer}}=MI, (10)

bytes, respectively. The separate path writes BF16, reads it again, and writes FP8. The producer path writes FP8 only once.

FuTransformer uses delayed per-tensor scaling. Invocation tt quantizes its output with the maximum collected during invocation t−1t-1. At the same time, the epilogue computes the current maximum magnitude for invocation t+1t+1. It can therefore process and store each fragment immediately. The kernel does not need to keep a full output row in memory on chip while waiting for a global maximum.

The scale state has three requirements. The first invocation must have a valid initial scale. A scale must also be defined for all-zero tensors. Concurrent request groups must keep separate scale states unless they are intentionally run together. Production use also needs saturation counters, because a sudden change in value range can make the previous scale unsuitable.

3.2.4 Packed prefill

For requests with lengths S1,…,SBS_{1},\ldots,S_{B}, padded execution processes B​maxb​SbB\max_{b}S_{b} rows. Packed execution processes only

Mpacked=∑b=1BSb.M_{\mathrm{packed}}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}S_{b}. (11)

A prefix-sum array maps each packed row to its request and token position. This mapping also defines attention boundaries and KV-cache locations. FuTransformer compiles separate kernels for padded and packed inputs, so the padded path does not need runtime layout checks.

3.3 Fragment-aligned INT4 decode

3.3.1 Why decode needs a different path

Let PP be the number of projection-weight elements in one layer. Excluding small metadata fields, the minimum number of bytes read during decode is

ℬdecode=P​w+2​B​T​Hk​v​D​k,\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{decode}}=Pw+2BTH_{kv}Dk, (12)

Here, ww is the number of bytes per weight, and kk is the number of bytes per cached K or V element. For the 8B shape at batch one, the projection weights contain 218.1 million elements. These weights occupy 436 MB in BF16, 218 MB in E4M3, or 109 MB in INT4. Reducing ww and kk therefore directly reduces the data that must be read and can lower latency.

On H100, the small-MM decode kernels cannot use an INT4 MMA that directly reads these packed values. They also have too few rows for the large FP8 WGMMA shapes used in prefill. FuTransformer therefore expands low-bit values into 16-bit MMA operands. Its layouts allow this expansion to happen while building the fragments, without a separate dequantization stage.

3.3.2 INT4 KV-cache mirror

FuTransformer keeps the BF16 KV cache as the main copy for prefill and compatibility, and maintains an INT4 copy for decode. Each byte stores two signed 4-bit values. Each token and KV head has one FP32 scale, calculated as amax/7\operatorname{amax}/7.

Scaling is performed outside the elementwise loop. For K, the scale is applied to the completed query–key dot product. For V, it is applied to the attention probability before the probability–value MMA. The kernel therefore avoids scaling each unpacked element separately.

A shared-memory table with 256 entries maps each packed byte to two FP16 values. One lookup expands both nibbles into the pair format needed by an MMA fragment. The table does not depend on the token scale, because scales are applied after accumulation.

Keys follow the byte order required by the B operand of mma.sync.m16n8k16. Each lane reads a contiguous segment the size of its fragment and uses byte-indexed lookups to fill the operand registers directly. This avoids creating a dequantized K tile and moving it through shared memory. V stays in natural channel order because the probability–value MMA groups values differently. It is transposed through shared memory before use.

The attention CTA quantizes the new cache row that it will use in the current decode step. The asynchronous-copy pipeline loads cache scales together with their K/V tile. This keeps cache updates and scale loads outside the serial inner attention loop.

3.3.3 Hadamard transform for cache outliers

Uniform INT4 quantization can lose accuracy when a few channels have large values. Following QuaRot and SAW-INT4 Ashkboos and others (2024); Jia et al. (2026), FuTransformer applies a normalized block-diagonal Hadamard matrix HH before writing each cache row. The query uses the same transform:

(H​q)⊤​(H​k)=q⊤​H⊤​H​k=q⊤​k.(Hq)^{\top}(Hk)=q^{\top}H^{\top}Hk=q^{\top}k. (13)

The attention output is transformed back once per query row. The transform uses a Walsh–Hadamard butterfly implemented with registers and warp shuffles. Each cache row is rotated once when it is written. The query and output are each rotated once per decode step. The attention loop therefore performs the same work per cached token, and the added rotation cost does not grow with context length. By default, each block covers the full head dimension, but narrower blocks can also be used.

3.3.4 INT4 projection weights

Weights are quantized offline with one symmetric scale for each output channel and each group of 128 input elements. The nibbles follow the order required by the B fragments of the decode MMA, so each warp can load a contiguous weight segment for its output tile. The format defines where each nibble is stored, not how its value is chosen. Values can come from the library’s round-to-nearest quantizer or a calibrated method such as GPTQ. Both quantization grids are packed into the same layout offline.

Weights are dequantized in registers. Each nibble is inserted into the mantissa bits of the BF16 value 128.0. A logic operation produces packed BF16 values of the form (128+n,128+m)(128+n,128+m). One packed BF16 fused multiply-add then subtracts 136. This removes the base value 128 and the offset of 8 used to convert an unsigned nibble to a signed value. Each group is accumulated separately. Its group scale is applied before the result is added to the running FP32 accumulator. The kernel never creates a full BF16 weight tile.

For M=1M=1, each warp reads the weights for one output tile and a quarter of the reduction dimension. The four warps in a CTA combine their partial sums through shared memory. For 2≤M≤322\leq M\leq 32, a skinny kernel loads activation tiles, packed weights, and scales through a multi-stage asynchronous-copy pipeline. It uses split-K across CTAs when additional CTAs are needed to keep the GPU occupied.

4 Evaluation

4.1 Experimental setup

We run the experiments on one NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5 GPU with CUDA 13.0 and PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130. For prefill and CODA measurements, the SM clock is fixed at 1980 MHz. Decode measurements use default clocks. We interleave the compared implementations within the same run so that they experience similar thermal conditions. Unless stated otherwise, compiled PyTorch and FuTransformer both use CUDA graphs. Prefill results are the median of four to eight timing invocations after warm-up. For CODA, we alternate the two binaries over three rounds. For decode, all PyTorch and FuTransformer candidates run in one process over three interleaved rounds. Both comparisons report median CUDA event time over repeated launches. Each table is a separate interleaved run, so the same configuration can differ by up to 2% between tables; each comparison is made within one table. The per-layer tests use synthetic inputs and weights, quantized with the library’s round-to-nearest quantizer. The whole-model tests in Section 4.5 use the trained checkpoint and the GPTQ-packed weights described in Section 4.8. The quantizer changes the nibble values but not their number or storage positions, so it does not change latency. The two quantizers give the same timing within run-to-run variation. The labels 1B, 8B, 70B, and 405B refer to layer shapes. They do not imply that a complete model of that size runs on one GPU.

The prefill baseline is a compiled, CUDA-graphed PyTorch block using torch._scaled_mm. It uses one activation scale per row and one weight scale per output channel. The baseline and FuTransformer both use FP8 projections and BF16 attention. We calculate effective prefill throughput from the projection FLOPs and causal-attention FLOPs:

P\displaystyle P =H⁡(Hq+2​Hk​v)​D+H​Hq​D+3​H​I,\displaystyle=H(H_{q}+2H_{kv})D+HH_{q}D+3HI, (14)
Fprefill\displaystyle F_{\mathrm{prefill}} ≈2​B​S​P+2​B​S2​Hq​D.\displaystyle\approx 2BSP+2BS^{2}H_{q}D. (15)

For decode, PyTorch provides an eager BF16 block and a compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 block. It does not provide a directly comparable full block that combines INT4 weights with an INT4 KV cache. We therefore state the precision of every decode result. We also compare FuTransformer’s BF16, FP8, and INT4 paths to measure the effect of reading fewer bytes within the same implementation.

4.2 Prefill compared with PyTorch

Figure 1 shows prefill at batch one. Speedup ranges from 0.92×\times to 1.48×\times across the tested configurations. The 1B shape at S=512S=512 is the only measured FP8 case where FuTransformer is slower than PyTorch. Avoiding intermediate activation reads and writes becomes more useful for larger shapes or longer sequences. The 405B layer reaches 1286 TFLOP/s at S=2048S=2048 and stays near 1.20–1.29 PFLOP/s across the measured range.

For the 8B shape at S=2048S=2048, FuTransformer takes 804.2 μ\mus, compared with 1004.5 μ\mus for PyTorch, giving a 1.25×\times speedup. This agrees with the design goal. The projection mainloop is already close to the library GEMM rate, so most of the improvement comes from avoiding intermediate activation traffic and separate conversion or cache-placement kernels.

4.3 Closest shared stage compared with CODA

CODA targets training and does not implement the same full inference block. A full-block comparison would therefore be misleading. We compare the closest shared operation instead: gate/up projection followed by SwiGLU. CODA runs linear_swiglu, and FuTransformer runs its gate/up epilogue. Both are tested on the same H100 using coda-kernels 0.3.1 with nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0.

Table 2 separates the two comparisons. Panel A is the main precision-matched comparison: compiled PyTorch, CODA, and FuTransformer all use BF16. Panel B places the final FuTransformer FP8 inference path beside the available BF16 baselines. This compares the final results, but the precisions differ. There is no CODA FP8 row because the released linear_swiglu fails an assertion when given FP8 operands on this GPU. Outside SM100 and SM120, its gated output must be 16-bit. In both panels, lower latency is better. Each speedup is the baseline latency divided by the FuTransformer latency in the same row.

In the precision-matched BF16 comparison, FuTransformer takes 613 μ\mus for 8B and 9442 μ\mus for 405B. This is 1.18×\times and 1.07×\times faster than compiled PyTorch, and 1.13×\times and 1.03×\times faster than CODA. At 8B, both implementations vary by less than 1% between rounds. At 405B, FuTransformer varies by 4%, and CODA ranges from 9355–11665 μ\mus. The 1.03×\times result is therefore within the measurement spread and should be treated as similar performance. With E4M3, our final inference path takes 316 μ\mus and 4819 μ\mus. The two APIs also perform slightly different work: FuTransformer applies the RMSNorm row scale, while CODA saves auxiliary data for backward computation. Table 2 therefore compares the closest shared stage, rather than the complete systems.

4.4 Decode compared with PyTorch

Table 3 compares the INT4 decode block with three PyTorch baselines. Two use BF16: the eager reference block and the same block compiled with CUDA graphs. The third matches the weight precision. It replaces the four projections in the same block with PyTorch’s INT4 weight-only kernel, torch._weight_int4pack_mm, using group size 128 and BF16 activations. This is the kernel used by gpt-fast and torchao. The INT4 block is compiled and CUDA-graphed in the same way. Normalization, RoPE, cache writes, residuals, and attention use the same code on both sides; only the projection kernels and cache format differ. All candidates run in one process over three interleaved rounds.

When both implementations use a BF16 cache, FuTransformer is 1.3–5.0×\times faster than the precision-matched INT4 block. This comparison isolates the projection kernels and fusion. With its INT4 cache copy, FuTransformer is 1.3–6.3×\times faster, and the gap is widest where PyTorch has no matching INT4 cache. The eager INT4 block takes 848–2604 μ\mus and is limited by launch overhead, as is the eager BF16 block. PyTorch’s INT4 kernel is tuned for a single query row, so its advantage over PyTorch’s own compiled BF16 block shrinks as rows are added: it is 1.6×\times faster at batch one on 8B, 2.2×\times faster at batch one on 70B, roughly even at batch 8, and 1.9–2.6×\times slower at batch 32. The strongest PyTorch baseline is therefore its INT4 block at small batch and its BF16 block at batch 32, and FuTransformer is 1.3–2.4×\times faster than whichever is faster in each row.

Table 4 varies batch size while keeping context fixed at 1024, so the two effects can be separated. FuTransformer’s INT4 latency stays nearly constant from one to eight sequences because reading the shared weights is still the bottleneck. Latency rises when projection computation becomes the bottleneck. PyTorch’s INT4 latency grows roughly linearly, from 106 to 585 μ\mus, because _weight_int4pack_mm uses a GEMV-shaped kernel for a single query row. From 16 sequences onward, it is slower than PyTorch’s compiled BF16 block, so BF16 becomes the stronger PyTorch baseline. Comparing with the faster PyTorch block at each point, FuTransformer achieves speedups of 1.4, 2.7, 2.3 and 2.1×\times across this range.

Table 5 tests every combination of projection-weight format (BF16, E4M3, INT4) and KV-cache format (BF16, E4M3 mirror, INT4 mirror) within FuTransformer. This helps separate precision effects from fusion. We use one library build for each cache format and interleave all candidates in one process. The three main decode paths are the diagonal entries: BF16 weights with a BF16 cache, E4M3 weights with an E4M3 cache copy, and INT4 weights with an INT4 cache copy. On this diagonal, INT4 is 31–51% faster than FP8 and 37–68% faster than BF16. At batch 8 or below and context 1024, changing the cache format changes latency by at most 2.5%, within run-to-run variation, because weight traffic dominates. At batch 32 and context 4096, the E4M3 cache saves 55–61 μ\mus and the INT4 cache 86–89 μ\mus, for every weight format. The gain is largest when projection-weight traffic dominates.

These speedups come from three sources: fewer weight bytes, fewer KV-cache bytes, and block fusion. The comparison with PyTorch therefore does not measure fusion alone. The within-FuTransformer table separates the first two effects. Lower weight precision reduces latency for every shape. Lower cache precision reduces latency when cache reads make up a large share of the total bytes.

4.5 Whole-model decode and prefill

Table 6 evaluates the complete Llama-3.1-8B model. Every decoder layer uses the fused block, while PyTorch runs the embedding, final RMSNorm, and LM head. We capture one greedy decode step in a single CUDA graph and replay it. The step takes a token as input and produces the next token. Its timing includes the 32 block launches and reads of the 1 GB BF16 LM-head weights, which are unchanged by the decode-weight format. The PyTorch baselines use the transformers implementation of the same BF16 checkpoint with a static cache, in eager mode or compiled with CUDA graphs. We time decode steps at positions just below the reported context length, using 64 steps per round for five rounds and reporting the median. Prefill uses one 2048-token prompt at batch one. INT4 is supported only for decode, so the INT4 rows use BF16 prefill.

The complete INT4 model decodes 2.0–2.2×\times faster than FuTransformer’s BF16 model at batch 8 or below, and 1.9×\times faster at batch 32 and context 4096. In the latter case, INT4 cache storage contributes about as much as INT4 weights. A step takes 11.7 ms with BF16 weights and cache, 8.8 with INT4 weights alone, and 6.0 with both. Compared with FuTransformer’s BF16 path, the whole-model gain is smaller than the per-layer gain in Table 3. At batch one, the embedding and LM head add about 0.3 ms to every path. Prefilling 2048 tokens takes 46 ms with BF16 and 27 ms with FP8, compared with 52 ms for compiled PyTorch.

The whole-model speedup over the transformers implementation is 2.9–9.9×\times, larger than the 2.1–2.9×\times in Table 3. Profiling the compiled PyTorch step explains this difference. At batch 32 and context 4096, attention accounts for 89% of its 60.8 ms step. Copy kernels take 29 ms to expand the 8 KV heads to the 32 query heads and arrange the cache for cuDNN. The cuDNN attention kernel takes another 23 ms to process the full 4096-entry static cache. Projections take 5.9 ms, close to 32 times the per-layer block. At batch one, projection GEMMs account for 81% of the step, and weight traffic explains the performance gap. The transformers static-cache attention path therefore takes about ten times as long as PyTorch SDPA on the compact cache used in the per-layer benchmark. FuTransformer reads its 8-head INT4 cache directly in fragment order, without expanding the heads. This explains most of the whole-model advantage. Table 6 uses BF16 PyTorch rows because transformers has no equivalent whole-model INT4 path available in this setup. The precision-matched kernel result is the per-layer comparison in Table 3; the whole-model ratio also includes these framework-level differences.

4.6 Design ablation

Table 7 uses compile-time switches to replace design elements of the INT4 decode block with earlier versions, while keeping precision and data size fixed. Storing K in natural order and transposing it through shared memory, rather than using the MMA fragment order in Section 3.3, increases latency by 16% at batch 32 and context 4096. It costs at most 2.3% where cache reads account for only a small share of the bytes. If per-nibble arithmetic also replaces the byte-indexed lookup, the combined latency increase is 25%. These two changes reproduce the earlier cache design. Quantizing the new cache row in a separate kernel between QKV and attention, rather than inside attention, adds 1–2 μ\mus per step. Converting weight nibbles with an extra bias MMA, instead of register logic and FMA operations, increases latency by 9% at batch one, 20% at batch 8, and 11% on 70B. The earlier FMA split-KV attention kernel takes 9–17% more time than the Tensor Core INT4-cache kernel at context 1024, and 2.4×\times as long at batch 32 and context 4096. The earlier skinny BF16 projection kernel does not support low-bit formats, so we compare it only on the BF16 path. For the three 8B shapes, its latencies are 192, 232 and 299 μ\mus, compared with 167, 174 and 276 for the current kernel.

4.7 Numerical results

We compare single-layer outputs with two references. Prefill tests use a separate FP64 implementation, and decode tests use the PyTorch BF16 block. These tests measure numerical error on synthetic data. Section 4.8 evaluates the INT4 weight path on a trained checkpoint.

Table 8 reports prefill RMSE at S=512S=512. On these synthetic inputs, the delayed-scale FP8 path has 1.8–2.0% higher RMSE than the PyTorch FP8 baseline with row-wise scales. The fused BF16 path has lower error. This is consistent with performing several operations between BF16 GEMMs in FP32, but this experiment does not measure that effect separately.

Table 9 summarizes decode error. On random data, the INT4 cache has about three times the RMS error of the E4M3 cache. INT4 weights follow the same trend. Increasing four K channels per head by 8×\times sharply raises the unrotated INT4 cache error. The Hadamard transform reduces this error from 22.2% to 7.4% for the 8B shape, and from 29.9% to 12.9% for the 1B shape.

The remaining INT4 error comes from quantization rather than a mismatch in the kernel implementation. The next subsection measures this error on a trained checkpoint and shows that GPTQ reduces it without changing the packed execution format. Under channel outliers, the rotated INT4 cache is much more accurate than the unrotated cache, although E4M3 remains more accurate.

4.8 INT4 decode on a trained checkpoint

The synthetic tests isolate kernel error. To measure the quality cost of the INT4 decode path on a real model, we evaluate the BF16 release of Llama-3.1-8B Grattafiori and others (2024) on the WikiText-2 test set Merity et al. (2017), following the GPTQ protocol Frantar et al. (2023). We concatenate the test split and divide it into 141 non-overlapping windows of 2048 tokens. Perplexity is the exponential of the mean token negative log-likelihood. Every token is decoded one position at a time through the production decode block of each of the 32 layers. PyTorch runs the embedding, final RMSNorm, and LM head, and 32 windows are decoded in parallel. Table 10 uses a BF16 KV cache to isolate weight quantization. Table 11 uses the INT4 cache copy and evaluates the complete INT4 decode block. GPTQ calibration uses 32 random windows of 2048 tokens from the WikiText-2 training split. GPTQ uses symmetric 4-bit weights, static groups of 128, no column reordering, 5% damping, and an FP64 error-feedback solve on the GPU. Using the WikiText-2 validation split, we selected round-to-nearest quantization for layer 1’s down projection, where Llama-3 forms the massive activations that later layers attend to Sun et al. (2024); the test split was used only to produce the reported numbers. An offline packer stores the GPTQ grid in the kernel layout and matches the library quantizer byte for byte. The kernels themselves are unchanged.

Table 10 shows the results. The BF16 kernel path matches PyTorch perplexity to three decimal places. For round-to-nearest weights, the INT4 kernel path and a BF16 simulated-quantization reference built from the same grid agree to 0.001 perplexity. Round-to-nearest INT4 weights increase perplexity by 0.99, while GPTQ weights in the same format increase it by 0.75. For this model, choosing each group’s scale with a mean-squared-error search, rather than the group maximum, makes round-to-nearest quantization less accurate.

Table 11 adds the INT4 KV-cache copy. Its last row therefore evaluates the complete INT4 decode block. With Hadamard rotation, the cache adds 0.15–0.23 perplexity beyond the weight-quantization cost, which is less than the cost of the weights themselves. The complete block with GPTQ weights reaches 7.18, or 0.94 above BF16. Without rotation, quantizing the cache alone adds 0.54, and the complete block reaches 7.76. Rotation therefore removes about 70% of the cache’s quality cost on the trained model. This agrees with the synthetic outlier results in Table 9.

Table 12 measures per-layer error in two ways. The independent tests evaluate one layer at a time, using the hidden state entering that layer in the BF16 model. We prefill 512 real tokens with BF16 weights, then decode four more real tokens with the block’s INT4 projections. The reference uses the same input and block with BF16 weights. BF16 kernels differ from an FP32 reference by 0.3–0.4%. Round-to-nearest INT4 adds 10–13% relative RMS error to a layer’s decode output, while GPTQ adds 4.5–7%. The cascaded tests decode 16 windows through the INT4 stack using its own residual stream and KV cache. The error after each layer therefore includes errors from earlier layers and token positions.

After layer 31, cascaded error is 36% with round-to-nearest weights and 26% with GPTQ. It reaches 42% and 30%, respectively, near layer 11, then decreases. Errors are nearly the same for positions 256–1023 and 1024–2047. For the output logits, KL divergence from the BF16 next-token distribution is 0.14 and 0.08 nats per token, respectively. The top-1 prediction matches BF16 for 83.5% and 88% of tokens.

4.9 The served path and downstream tasks

Tables 10 and 11 decode every token from the start of each window. This isolates the decode path, but differs from the serving workflow. Table 13 evaluates that workflow. The first 1024 tokens of each window use BF16 or E4M3 prefill, since INT4 is supported only for decode. The remaining 1023 positions are decoded one at a time. We score only the decoded positions, and the cache copy contains all positions.

In the serving workflow, the complete INT4 decode block adds 0.53 perplexity, or 9.4% over the all-BF16 path. When every token is decoded from the first position, the increases are 0.94 and 15.1%. The protocols differ in two ways. In the serving test, each scored token has at least 1024 tokens of context, and the first half of the window is processed with higher-precision weights. FP8 prefill adds only 0.004 perplexity, and E4M3 decode weights add 0.02. Thus, the INT4 decode weights account for the full quality cost with either prefill path.

Perplexity does not directly measure task accuracy, so Table 14 adds two multiple-choice benchmarks. These evaluations score each answer option with a single forward pass rather than a decode loop, so they cannot use the decode kernels directly. We instead use a PyTorch model carrying the values the kernels compute with. The packed weights are dequantized and returned to the checkpoint’s original layout, and hooks quantize K and V for each token and head as the cache copy stores them, with one amax/7\operatorname{amax}/7 scale per token and head and K rotated first. For the weights this is the same simulated quantization that agrees with the kernel path to 0.001 perplexity; the cache hooks follow the kernel’s definition but were not separately cross-checked at this model size. INT4 weights reduce accuracy by 2.1 percentage points on HellaSwag and 4.9 on ARC-Challenge. The INT4 cache adds losses of 0.4 and 2.7 points, respectively. Repeating the two INT4 configurations independently changes the results by at most 0.3 points, within the standard errors of 0.4 and 1.5 points. ARC-Challenge shows a larger quality loss than perplexity alone suggests. The format increases perplexity by 15% in the all-decode test and 9% in the serving test, and reduces accuracy by up to 7.6 points on the harder of the two tasks.

4.10 Variable-length prefill

Table 15 compares packed and padded execution within FuTransformer for the 8B shape, with B=8B=8 and Smax=2048S_{\max}=2048. For equal-length inputs, packing adds no visible overhead. When one request has length 2048 and the other seven have length 128, packed execution is 5.07×\times faster because it skips most padded projection rows.

5 Discussion and Limitations

Baseline precision.

The PyTorch prefill comparison uses the same projection and attention precisions, but different activation-scaling policies. The BF16 gate/up comparison between FuTransformer and CODA is the closest like-for-like result, although their training and inference APIs keep different auxiliary data. The comparison between INT4 decode and the PyTorch BF16 reference uses different precisions: the reference has BF16 weights and a BF16 cache. Comparing BF16, FP8, and INT4 within FuTransformer isolates the effect of storage precision.

Scope.

Performance tests cover a single Transformer layer on one H100 and the complete Llama-3.1-8B model in Section 4.5. The quality tests in Section 4.8 use the same complete model. These tests do not include multi-layer scheduling, distributed communication, request admission, or complete serving latency. The 405B label describes one layer’s dimensions; we do not run a full 405B model on one GPU.

Accuracy.

Synthetic tests cover one layer. Trained-checkpoint tests cover one model, one dataset for perplexity, and two zero-shot multiple-choice tasks for accuracy. INT4 decode increases perplexity by 9–15%, depending on the protocol, and reduces ARC-Challenge accuracy by up to 7.6 percentage points. This is a meaningful quality loss. Delayed FP8 scaling is tested on stable workloads after warm-up. Production use also needs safe scale initialization, saturation monitoring, and request-local state. Task accuracy on trained checkpoints must still be validated before deployment.

Portability.

The implementation is designed for Hopper fragment layouts, asynchronous copies, and resource limits. Supporting another GPU generation requires different tile shapes, pipelines, and packed layouts. The main principles can still be applied, but the kernel details depend on the architecture.

6 Conclusion

FuTransformer optimizes prefill and decode separately. Prefill keeps FP8 GEMM throughput high and reduces data movement between operations. It extends CODA’s GEMM-plus-epilogue formulation with inference-specific cache placement, fixed RMSNorm-gain folding, delayed FP8 producer output, and packed inputs. Decode reads fewer bytes by using INT4 weights and an INT4 KV-cache copy. Both formats follow the layout required by the consuming MMA fragments, so values are dequantized close to where the Tensor Cores use them.

On one H100, FuTransformer prefill is up to 1.48×\times faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For the closest shared BF16 gate/up–SwiGLU stage, FuTransformer is 1.13×\times faster than CODA at the 8B shape. Over the 8B and 70B shapes at batch 1 to 32, the INT4 decode block is 1.3–2.4×\times faster than the stronger of PyTorch’s two decode blocks at each point. Measured separately, it is 2.1–3.3×\times faster than the compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 block and 1.3–6.3×\times faster than the same block using PyTorch’s INT4 projection kernel. It is also 31–51% faster than FuTransformer’s FP8 path. The complete 8B model decodes 2.9×\times faster than compiled PyTorch at batch one. On Llama-3.1-8B, INT4 weights increase WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.99 with round-to-nearest quantization or 0.75 with GPTQ in the same format. The rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20, giving a complete INT4 block that is 0.94 above BF16. Without rotation, quantizing the cache alone would add 0.54. The kernel path matches a simulated-quantization reference to within 0.001 perplexity. These results support GEMM epilogues for prefill and fragment-aligned low-bit execution for decode.
